articles.title: WALKING IN THE SPIRIT
articles.author: C. R. Byng
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Plainfield, N.J.

paragraphs.text: The apostle brings in this exhortation as part of the positive way in which he sought to help the brethren in Galatia who had moved away from a system of power into an outward order of things. The general teaching of the epistle shows that the liberty of sonship is one of the great thoughts that is in the mind of God, but in the working out of it the apostle does not exactly bring in the matter of walking in the liberty of sonship, but of walking in the Spirit.

Walking in the Spirit would be the way in which the liberty of sonship would be maintained, and opens up thus an order of liberty and power which is in no way related to this world’s system of things connected with “flesh’s lust” and “the works of the flesh” (Galatians 5: 19).

Other scriptures remind us of the scope of things which are characterised by being “in the Lord” and “in the Christ”. “In the Lord” involves a system of authority where the rights of the Lord Jesus are honoured in a way which brings in sanctification and help. “In the Christ” brings in a system of things where the divine Operator is working in relation to the filling out of the divine thoughts, as the apostle says, “God, who always leads us in triumph in the Christ”, 2 Corinthians 2: 14. That is related to a sphere where Christ is working out everything for the glory of God.

But “walk in the Spirit” involves a more intimate area. Authority must be related to it, and yet it opens up a sphere of power and liberty and joy. So that the first three features of the fruit of the Spirit, the result of walking in the Spirit, are love, joy, peace (Galatians 5: 22). This is not the outward matters which would flow out of that, but the inward fruit of walking in the Spirit is primarily what is secured Godward in relation to love, joy, peace. The Spirit peculiarly enters into this, as it says, “the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5: 5), and as walking in the Spirit, beloved brethren, we prove the reality of the expansion of the love of God. You cannot link anything small with the love of God. The love of God is to fill a universe eternally for God, and walking in the Spirit means that we are enlarged in love toward God.

There is also the side of joy, not joy in filling out the lusts of the flesh, but joy in relation to what is for God, and as we are helped to walk in the Spirit, the Spirit of God will open up to us increasingly all the vast area of things where God Himself is able to rejoice.

It is a feature of the eternal realm that God will “rejoice over thee with joy” (Zephaniah 3: 17), but the reality of walking in the Spirit is to bring us into the anticipation of the joy that is to fill eternity. It is one of the services of the Spirit of God that He brings us into the reality of the experience of what will fill eternity without limitation, interruption or diversion. It will not be something different, for He brings us into the enjoyment at the present time of what is to be enjoyed eternally. The fulness and the character and the power of it are the same, but at the present time there are the frailty of the flesh and the limitations of time. Matters come in so that the enjoyment of what is eternal in principle may have to be interrupted in some sense by other matters, but the joy that is related to walking in the Spirit is really the joy that is to fill the new heavens and the new earth for the pleasure of God. It is thus joy Godward.

Another feature of the fruit of walking in the Spirit is that the saints can be preserved in peace Godward in the midst of a world where there is trouble and sorrow and strife. This is even more extensive than that because the apostle brings this in where there were disturbances as to the truth. The setting of the epistle is unusual in that it is addressed to the assemblies of Galatia. It is not to the assembly, as in Corinth, Ephesus, Philippi, and Colosse, but to the assemblies of Galatia, showing that there had been some influence affecting more than one local assembly and that would tend to bring in disturbance and unrest. But walking in the Spirit would preserve the saints in the peace that is related to the liberty of sonship. There is power in the Spirit to be maintained in what is for God, for the Spirit would serve so that the saints are preserved in response Godward in the service of God, and too in the testimony so that this is not affected by difficulties that the enemy might seek to bring in. The Spirit of God would thus maintain us in the liberty of communion with the Father. The dignity and power of sonship is to find expression in what is for God in the filling out in our hearts and in our lives and in our assembly experiences of the features of love, joy and peace.

The Spirit of God would encourage us to make way for His own personal power that characterises this great realm that is referred to here as ‘walking in the Spirit’. May He help us in this way, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: RECOVERY
articles.author: R. N. Hesterman
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Plainfield, N.J.

paragraphs.text: These scriptures are well known to the brethren. I could have read the whole section, but the thought I had in mind was how this man came to be recovered. Luke carries the thought of recovery through the book, and this man was proceeding in a wrong direction but was turned around. The two on the way to Emmaus were in a similar situation; they were conversing, and going in a wrong direction, and the Lord intervened. I was thinking of Proverbs 4: 26,
“Ponder the path of thy feet”; and again “There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof is the ways of death”, Proverbs 14: 12.

The official side is alluded to in this section, the priest and the Levite, but I was thinking of the service of the Lord Jesus. John the baptist, beholding Jesus as He walked, said, “Behold the Lamb of God”, the One upon whom the Spirit descended. The Spirit descended upon Christ in order that He should take up a place of service. Think of the greatness of Christ in His own ministry! Although it could be said that it was without much outward result, it looked on to Paul’s ministry—a ministry from Christ as ascended. The greatest aspect of Christ’s service was what was for God. On the cross He said, “It is finished”. Think of the greatness of the work He accomplished; then His stoop into death and the grave. What greater service could there be, as He said, “No one has greater love than this, that one should lay down his life for his friends”, John 15: 13.

So the Samaritan here in Luke 10 has affection. It is not the official side, the Samaritan is the side of affection—a person who was ready to stoop down and bring in the necessary ingredients, the oil and wine, and pour them in. We think of how the Lord poured out His blood without reservation, and of how the water flowed. How great it is that this unique pouring out met the requirements of a righteous God as to sins and our sinful state. But here it is the pouring in of oil and wine, and it is open to each one of us to do this, as we see persons set on a wrong course. Of primary importance is our own individual responsibility. “Ponder the path of thy feet” means that in the christian pathway we are concerned as to where we are going. We may seem to be taking the right direction, saying or doing right things, perhaps being very active. In our private circumstances we may be on a course that seems to be very legitimate, but “There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof is the ways of death”.

The Lord would speak to us as to our pathway. I would certainly take it to myself that perhaps my feet are taking me where they should not. We have in mind one who lost consciousness and was in a coma for a while. We may enter into a position of temporary death. The Lord, in His grace, has recovered each one of us from that. It may be a matter of only a short time, but think of a man going away from Jerusalem! He is leaving the area of the service of God—where persons can be serviceable in Jerusalem. Think of Daniel (Daniel 6: 10), who prayed with his windows open toward Jerusalem. We pray to God that His service might be enriched. We pray, too, for our brother,

that he might be physically recovered, but all our prayers should have in mind a greater response in praise to God. In Malachi 3: 8 Jehovah asks, “Will a man rob God?” It is a matter of where our feet take us, in principle; and it bears on what we are able to take into the house of God; what we can carry in there as the fruit of individual experience, and pondering is really a background to this. John the baptist must have pondered the feet of Christ. He must have done that as he watched Him walk, and then he exclaimed, “Behold the Lamb of God”, John 1: 36. It must have been a very wonderful experience to get that impression of Christ.

The simple exercise I have is that our own feet should take us into the area where God can be served in a fuller way. This bears on our practical lives, as our brother was saying, and on our part together in testimony. As we are in relation to one another we may see one turning in a direction that is away from Jerusalem, and see the need to bring in the necessary ingredients, to bring in spiritual food. Indeed we are very thankful that we can assemble together and come under the authority of the word of God, what the Spirit would say in our time. It is a very great privilege to be able to do this, which many do not enjoy. As individual christians they have their links with the Lord, they have the Spirit perhaps, but how good it is to draw on one another. It says, “If they fall, the one will lift up his fellow”, Ecclesiastes 4: 10. The idea of “two or three” is a wonderful thought. So may we be helped to encourage one another, to ponder our own pathway, so that we are able to pick others up and assist in recovery. It is really God’s own doing, but He uses persons to serve in many different ways.

We are in the day of small things. Bethlehem typifies the assembly in its local expression, and in Micah it is said to be ‘little’, yet the Spirit would not occupy us with its littleness but rather with what comes out of it for God. He would have our minds and affections rest on these words, “Out of thee shall he come forth unto me …” That refers, of course, to the actual incoming of the Lord Jesus, for He was born in Bethlehem. No human mind can compass the infinite delight that God found in that Babe, and in the life of Jesus in its absolute perfection and moral excellence. Our brother has reminded us of the oblation in Leviticus 2, the first part being for God and the remainder for the priesthood. What choice food for our souls! The Lord Jesus is now in glory and we are here, set in different localities, many small, none very large, and the Holy Spirit is actively operating that Christ should be formed and expressed in us, and that primarily is for the pleasure of God. It is a great matter then that, in days of such outward smallness, our localities can yield much that is precious to the heart of God as Christ in character is expressed in us.

In 2 Samuel 23 it is the same place, Bethlehem. David is in the cave of Adullam, with the Philistines encamped in the valley of Rephaim, and he longs for a drink of the water of the well of Bethlehem.
These three mighty men who break through and bring David water represent what has the character of an affectionate assembly response now. Christ is in rejection, and He feels it.

What is Philistine is entrenched in the public position, and He feels that too, the heartless formality of mere religion, so cold and unresponsive. He has great regard then for those places where there are faithful brethren, fully identified with Him in His reproach, walking in true separation and exercised to be marked by the moral features of the assembly. Such know the Spirit and the limitless resources in Him. As near to Christ, He imparts to them a sense of His longings, and they, in love for Him, are prepared to overcome every obstacle and draw upon the exhaustless depths of the Spirit’s resources to provide a fresh, living response in assembly affection to meet the longings of His heart. Surely He is worthy! The Lord Jesus really appreciates such response. Indeed, it is touching that what the saints provide is taken up and used by Christ in what is so precious to His heart, the service of God.

In Genesis 43 it is Benjamin, and there is a close link between Benjamin and Bethlehem, for he must have been born near it (see Genesis 35: 16–18). In Psalm 68: 27 he is called “little Benjamin”. He was like Joseph, having the same mother, and the place that he had in Joseph’s affections is indicated in his portion being “five times greater than the portions of them all”. He reminds us of the disciple whom Jesus loved. At times Joseph’s dealings with his brethren seemed rough, but he knew what he was after, that Benjamin should come to light. And so it is that at times Christ’s dealings with us seem to be severe, but His objective is that He should see Himself morally in us. Benjamin represents “He that overcomes”.

There is much to overcome today and as we consider what is held out to such in Revelation 2 and 3 there is great incentive to be overcomers. What is offered is like Benjamin’s portion. It says here that Joseph had portions carried to them “from before him”, which suggests to us that what we get is fresh, that with which the Lord Jesus is currently engaged, which becomes the food of those who are pleasing to Him.

Well, dear brethren, the days of reproach and smallness publicly will soon be over; the opportunity of ministering assembly-wise to the pleasure of God and the heart of Christ in a hostile world will soon be gone for ever, never to be repeated. May our concern be that our localities may yield increasingly for the pleasure of God, and may we have a deepening sense of the Lord’s approval in an abundant flow of spiritual food.

The Lord Jesus is referred to in Matthew 13 as a Man who has found something, but He could not possess it without selling something. Matthew’s gospel brings out, as we know, the King, King of righteousness, King of Salem, King of peace. His kingship is established in the genealogical line from Abraham through David, affording full proof of the kingship of Christ, the Messiah, from that point of view. What rights the Lord Jesus had, and yet it says here that He found something that required a transaction in selling.

Previously in this gospel His ministry is rejected and He turns to the Father and says, “I praise thee, Father, Lord of the heaven and of the earth, that thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to babes” (Matthew 11: 25). The Roman system at that time was not good enough to contain Christianity, neither was the Grecian, or any other administration under the hand of man. Christianity was too great for them, but for the Lord to possess the world and the treasure in it required the transaction in which He sold all whatever He had. What did He sell? He gave up His rights to kingship—“Is it at this time that thou restorest the kingdom to Israel?”, Acts 1: 6. No, it was not at that time; He gave that up.

Why did He give it up? On account of you and me. There was on this earth a treasure that He desired to possess because He loved it. Never forget that Christ loved the assembly and delivered Himself up for it (Ephesians 5: 25). It was not the other way round. He did not deliver Himself up for it in order that He might love it.

So here in this section He sells all whatever He had and buys that field. He has possession of the world. Did you know that? The whole thing is His. It does not look like it publicly at the present time, but we are in the secret of the fact that it is His; not only creationally but also by redemption He has secured rights to the whole world and all that is in it is His. Were you hid in that world? Yes, you were hid in it and He found you; I was hid in it and He found me.

What a thing it is that you have been found by Christ. He sells all that He has and buys that field. He waits for the day of glory, but He is securing out of this world a people for a possession. The way He does it is His own way, His own handiwork.

I want to touch briefly on two cases where the Lord secures persons. The Lord finds Philip and says, “Follow me”. There was no resistance in Philip; he followed Him. Philip finds Nathaniel who does not say much that is of credit as to Christ. He says, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”; but he was a man in whom there was no guile. We might have thought that he should have had a knowledge of the truth of what was going to come out of Nazareth, but it seems as if he did not. The Lord was not put off by the first reaction in the man. Grace in Christ was flowing through Philip, and Nathaniel is brought to Christ. Philip does not take up the argument; he says, “Come and see”. What an invitation, and what a lesson on how to meet people. The Lord says to the apostles, “He that believes on me, the works which I do shall he do also, and he shall do greater than these”, John 14: 12. Mr. Taylor remarked that although the works may be greater, they were not done as He did them.

How the Lord did things belonged distinctively to Himself, the manner of the doing belonged to Deity (J.T. N.S. Vol. 40, pp. 241–243). The manner of the doing—how He did things in this chapter—captivated Nathaniel securely for Himself. His own touch enters into the lives of every one of us, captivating our hearts for Him and for Him alone.

So Philip says, “Come and see”. When a person comes to the meeting, even though there may have been resistance, God may be working. We have to credit persons who come with that, that God may be working and drawing them to Himself. There may be very little outwardly, but if they come they have ceased to be an object to themselves and it may be that Christ is becoming an object to them.

Whether they are in orbit as yet may not be known to us, but they may be moving into orbit. Who would hinder a soul that is coming into his orbit, into relation to Christ? The Lord Jesus does not. He does not say, Nathaniel, what was that you said of Me, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” He says, “One truly an Israelite, in whom there is guile”. That is Christ’s valuation of him. Let us get God’s valuation of persons, not our own.

Then Nathaniel says, “Whence knowest thou me?” What a question to put to the Son of God; what a question to put to Jesus! Think of what he had been told—“We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the law, and the prophets”. Yet the Lord does not upbraid him for it. He says, “Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig-tree, I saw thee”. The disclosure of the Person affects Nathaniel’s heart. He says, “Rabbi, thou art the Son of God, thou art the King of Israel”. How He broke him down! Let us learn from Christ.

Regarding the woman in John 4 the same thing comes to light. She says to the Lord, “How dost thou, being a Jew, ask to drink of me who am a Samaritan woman? for Jews have no intercourse with Samaritans”. Did the conversation close then? Let us search our hearts; would we have closed the conversation? Would we regard it as hopeless? But He goes on.

What does it bring out in the woman? Respect for the Person. That is why I read where three times she says, “Sir”. There was coming out in that woman respect for the Person. It comes out through the presentation of the One who dispenses the living water. The Lord brings it in, that word as to living water, and she says, “Sir, give me this water”.

The moral history is settled and then she says, “Sir, I see that thou art a prophet”. How the light dawns in her soul! Do we know about it personally, how the light dawns in our souls in regard of Christ and who He is? Have you never been through it personally? Experiences similar to these which this woman had result in something entering into the fabric of your soul so that you can go and say, “Come, see a man who told me all things I had ever done—is not he the Christ?” And persons are affected by it. It is a challenge to us at the present time as to whether that is so. The Lord says to His disciples, “The fields … are already white to harvest” (John 4: 35). I wonder whether I see that. Coming down here along the motorways we saw the fields white to harvest and the machines working in them. Does that not bring out something of what God is going to reap?

James is a pungent apostle who does not mince his words. It is understood that James’ epistle may have been written early but what he says goes down the dispensation. “My brethren, if any one among you err from the truth, and one bring him back”. One cannot read this section without it bringing to mind the remarkable address by Mr. Taylor, ‘The Conversion of a Sinner’ (N.S. Vol. 13, p.410). I wonder if the spirit of what that man spoke about those many years ago has permeated our souls as to the conversion of a sinner, a sinner among the brethren, “If any one among you err from the truth”. How many there are who have erred from the truth presently. But you and I are searched, and I feel it for myself right to the core of my being as to whether I am among those who can bring back one—“and one bring him back”. Oh, can we bring back? You see how grace flowed in Christ to meet those to whom we have referred. Grace flowed in; it was not put off by the initial contact; grace upon grace flowed in. Grace is first in the transaction; truth is the ultimate. Oh, can we turn one back from the error of his ways in relation to the truth, save a soul from death, and cover a multitude of sins? Does everything have to be brought out in public? No, it does not. Things can be covered privately, but the ground that is secured for God is the treasure that is hid in the field now brought into circulation.

The heart of the father was moved when he saw that son rise up in Luke 15. How do you know when change has taken place? When he rose up in his filthy rags there initially God had worked in his soul and a change had taken place. When persons move, when they come, a change may be taking place. Can we be of value and of help to such? How do you get guidance or wisdom, as James says? “The wisdom from above first is pure, then peaceful, gentle, yielding, full of mercy and good fruits, unquestioning”. It is not contentious. Philip was not contentious. The Lord Jesus did not contend with Nathaniel or the woman. He brought in the truth and He attracted persons to Himself. That is how to work. Grace is not contentious. Grace does not miss things, but it is not contentious. It does not get at the contentious points. Grace gets behind the contention and reaches the work of God in a man so as to bring him back to Christ. “If any one among you err from the truth, and one bring him back …” How are you going to get behind the difficulty? Reach the man, reach the soul in the man, bring him to establish communion with Christ, so that he is brought back from the error of his ways.

The glad tidings go forth each Lord’s day and many weary souls are converted. That is true, thank God, but there is a need for converters amongst us. I do not know the situation that exists in this place altogether; you do not know the situation that exists in Edinburgh; but I am searching my heart as to whether I have definitely committed myself to seek to bring back one from the error of his ways, or whether I have been put off by an initial reception on a door-step. Oh, there is searching of the heart with God as to whether we may have been put off by the initial thing and yet underneath there is the work of God. How can we bring him back? There is toil in it. You need to be with God in it, to seek wisdom, but the Psalm says, “Light is sown for the righteous”, Psalm 97: 11. What a thing that is! It says in this scripture, “The fruit of righteousness in peace is sown for them that make peace”. Wisdom is there in God; wisdom is available to us, flowing pure and unstinted from God its source. God will sow light for a righteous man and joy for the upright in heart. We can count on God to sow light for righteous persons enabling them to become converters. If we have known what it is to be converted, we can be on the way to being converters. What do we know of being saved from the error of our ways? Who brought us back? Who served us in the Spirit of Christ in the presence of all our objections and brought us back? Somebody reached what was real, that treasure hid in a field. What a field it is! What a harvest it is going to be! Let us lift up our eyes and see that the fields are already white to harvest.

We come in this sense into the divine economy under Christ and the Spirit, usable in the hands of divine Persons so as to secure persons and turn them back from the error of their ways. “My brethren, if any one among you err …” How that reaches the affections of our hearts, because we have known and loved brethren, walked to the house of God and enjoyed communion with them, and yet it may be that they have erred from the truth. Who can bring them back into the enjoyment of that sweet communion?

Well, these are real and true things. The Lord has delight in persons who are exercised thus. It is labour and toil, and communion with God is required to seek the wisdom from above. One feature of wisdom which ought to come to light in a person who is a converter is that he is peaceful, he has not come to make war; he is gentle, he is not coming to irritate; he is yielding, he is prepared to understand something of the difficulty; he is full of mercy—why?

because he has been shown mercy. Oh what a thing to be full of mercy because you have been shown mercy. And he is unquestioning; that is, he is not contentious. He is unfeigned, no mixed motives, “but the fruit of righteousness in peace is sown for them that make peace”.
The scripture says, “Blessed the peace-makers, for they shall be called sons of God”, Matthew 5: 9. Well, dear brethren, may the Lord help us to be on these lines, for His name’s sake.

It is interesting to see the different lines of teaching that come out in the epistles written by the apostles Paul and Peter and others. If we take, for instance, the Epistle to the Ephesians, I think we see some of the fruit of the apostle’s labours with them, how he for three whole years laboured night and day with tears.

But what he is able to say to them in his epistle seems to point to a high level of things in the service of God. Then we have Colossians, which is somewhat similar but perhaps not on quite such a high level. Then we have Corinthians, which is corrective, and we might say the same as to Galatians. Then in Romans we have more what is individual, what is fundamental.

We might wonder, perhaps, just what may be in mind in the Epistle to the Hebrews. It does not even mention the name of the writer, although I think we generally gather it was Paul who wrote it; but we might just wonder what the theme of that epistle is. I believe one of the things that comes out in a very striking way in that epistle, which perhaps we do not get anywhere else, is as to going into the holiest. We have had those amongst us who have known something in a real way of what it is to go into the holiest, and I believe the Lord would speak to us about that, because it is a very vital matter.

It would seem from these verses that going into the holiest involves three things—the first would be the perfect work of atonement; then, secondly, the present place of Christ on high, and, thirdly, our state, which I believe is vital to it. The first two are fixed, first, the efficacy of the Lord’s blood. It says, “The blood of Jesus, the new and living way which he has dedicated for us through the veil, that is, his flesh”. How precious it is to think of the perfect work of the Lord Jesus, what He has done; nothing can interfere with the effect of what has been completed by the perfect work of the Lord Jesus, the shedding of His blood and the giving of His body, so that we can go through the veil. How marvellous that is! Nothing can interfere with that. Then, too, as we think of the Lord’s present position on high, nothing can interfere with that.

It says, “Having a great priest over the house of God”, and I think this is the only place where the Scriptures speak about “a great priest”. There are several references to the Lord as High Priest, and “a great high priest” (Hebrews 4: 14), but I think this is the only reference where it says, “a great priest”. I think there is something precious about it, because it speaks about something that is unique to Christ. Aaron was high priest, but he was not “a great priest”. I think it is wonderful to think of Jesus in that way as the great Priest over the house of God, and our drawing near in the way of entering into the holy of holies is related to that, the place that Christ has. I think the end of chapter 6 of this epistle would bear on this. It speaks about an anchor “secure and firm, and entering into that within the veil, where Jesus is entered as forerunner for us” (Hebrews 6: 19, 20). It is very wonderful to think of it. I am reminded sometimes of a remark made in London in 1953 that when we go into the holiest we find that Jesus is there. That is a wonderful thing. I think we do well to test ourselves as to how much we know about it. I feel very humbled as to it, but how wonderful it is!

When we come to this third point, it says, “Let us approach with a true heart, in full assurance of faith, sprinkled as to our hearts from a wicked conscience, and washed as to our body with pure water”. That brings in our side. In that way it is not so fixed. I believe that normally it would be a settled matter. As we are right in our souls, right with God, we would know what it is in a practical way to be sprinkled as to our hearts from a wicked conscience and washed as to our body with pure water. That would prepare us for communion, and I believe this matter of entering into the holiest is a matter of communion. The two things are very much bound up together, not that they are identical, because I believe that if our state is right, as we are right with God, we can be in communion all the time. I believe that is normal christianity.

But going into the holiest is something which we do not do all the time. I believe it is right to say that. It is something that we have the privilege to do, but there are other matters that we have to attend to and so we do not go into the holiest all the time. At the same time, the two things are connected, the question of our going into the holiest and the question of communion, because it is evident that if we are not in communion then we cannot go into the holiest. I believe that is one thing that would have to be faced. But how encouraging it is to think of what is available to us, to think of the preciousness of the blood of Jesus and the “living way which he has dedicated for us through the veil, that is, his flesh”. How precious it is to think of that, and then the Lord’s position now on high, to think of how the Father would delight to bring Him before us and how as, in any measure, we go into the holiest we see Jesus there and have some impression of who He is, the One who is living now. Think of His place on high, “a great priest over the house of God”.
How it would encourage us not to be caught up with things that are around us, the features of the world. There is the religious world and the secular world, the religious world bringing in all

kinds of things that would interfere with what is due to God. We might be liable to be caught up with that kind of thing. Then there is the secular side, which is all around us. You see, I might say to myself, Well, I would not commit a murder and I would not steal; but perhaps I may say as to certain things that there is no harm in them. Well now, if I am on that line it is a question of whether I am in communion; it rather suggests lack of communion. I believe these are real things and that we need to face them. We do not want to go in for what is permissive. How much there is around which suggests permissiveness. I believe that if our minds are on that line, all we can say as to it is that we are not in communion.

So we need to face up to these things. I believe that the Lord would have us to be real, and to get before God about these things, if anything comes into our minds that is not just quite in line. So it says, “Let us approach with a true heart, in full assurance of faith”. Now I believe we need to have faith as to what has been done, faith as to the perfection of the work of Christ, faith as to His position now. That enters into it, but then, “Sprinkled as to our hearts from a wicked conscience, and washed as to our body with pure water”, involving what our walk might be, what we might do with our bodies. These are practical matters as to things that, if allowed, interrupt our communion. I believe the Lord would help us; He has given us the Spirit, and it says, “walk in the Spirit, and ye shall no way fulfil flesh’s lust”, Galatians 5: 16. We have been given the gift of the Spirit; we have power that way, so we do not need to be influenced by what is around, and what is within. That being settled, as we make use of the Spirit, being “sprinkled as to our hearts from a wicked conscience, and washed as to our body with pure water”, we are perfectly free to be in communion.

As all this comes before us, as our hearts are in full assurance of faith as we think of the finished work of Christ and His present position in glory, then, having overcome through the power of the Spirit, we are not only in communion but we are also at liberty to know something of what it is to enter the holiest. This is a very practical thing. It is perhaps something that we do not give very much attention to, but I believe it is very practical indeed and that what is for God at the present time depends on the extent to which we know what it is to go into the holiest. I trust that we may be encouraged. I trust we may also be searched. I myself feel very humbled as to it; I believe the Lord would search us and bring about reality so that there may be something more formed, something genuine, something which really answers to the heart of Christ and is for the pleasure of God. So may the Lord encourage us and bless the word, for His name’s sake.

There are frequent references in John’s gospel to the present day, the time of the Spirit, being anticipated, to which the Lord Jesus looked forward, we might say, with joy because of what it would mean to Himself and to the Father. So to the woman in John 4 the Lord speaks of the hour that is “coming and now is” (John 4: 23). The living water would be a reality in the Spirit’s day and the Father would have worshippers in spirit and truth, already anticipated in the Lord’s words and the satisfaction He received from the lonely woman of Sychar’s well.

In John 7 the water, a type of the Spirit, is not so much springing up as flowing out, the Lord’s words pointing to the Spirit’s day, as the writer indicates—“But this he said concerning the Spirit, which they that believed on him were about to receive; for the Spirit was not yet, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7: 39). Note that the word for believing—“he that believes on me”—is continuous present; so do we in faith embrace the advantages and prove the resources of the Spirit’s day?—for the Spirit has now come and here abides. Out of the belly of one believer, one who comes to Christ and drinks, can flow rivers, not just a river or stream, of living water. What an effect one such would have upon others!
Kingston, Ont.
PEACE-MAKERS There is—and always has been—a great need for peace-makers. James says, “The fruit of righteousness in peace is sown for them that make peace” (James 3: 18).

So approved are they of God that the Lord says of them in Matthew 5: 9, “they shall be called sons of God”. We may try to secure righteous ends by words or actions that are unwise, impetuous, or impatient. The peace-maker does his work in a restful, calm, and patient way, moving in the power of the wisdom from above which “first is pure, then peaceful, gentle, yielding, full of mercy and good fruits, unquestioning, unfeigned”, James 3: 17. Such are effective. They are honoured by a divine answer—“righteousness in peace” is sown for them. May we have grace to approach difficulties in the spirit of the peace-maker.

It is instructive to study peace-makers of old as they moved into difficult and delicate situations—for instance, Abraham’s firm, but gracious, handling of Abimelech in Genesis 21; Gideon’s skilful dealing with Ephraim’s unjust complaint in Judges 8, and David’s resolution of a tense, situation in 1 Samuel 30: 21–25 as to the division of the spoil of battle. In all these cases a peace-maker operated in the wisdom from above and we see the resulting fruit—“righteousness in peace”; peace is established and right principles upheld.

An overcomer then is one, we judge, who, in the midst of the corruptions indicated as existing in the assembly, maintains in the energy of the Spirit faithfulness to the Lord in holiness of walk and conduct. Realising the supremacy of the Lord’s claims he seeks at all cost to acquire a Nazarite condition, and he pursues this end whatever the obloquy, reproach or persecution he may have to encounter.
